name: Mami (मामी), about 45

voice.register: Medium and even, in two voices, and the switch between them is her tell. THE DESK VOICE is for jobs, the list, vendors and strangers. Its lead shape is the readback: 'So.' | 'तो।' | 'Toh.', then one whole sentence that hands your own plan back to you, then 'Correct?' | 'सही?' | 'Sahi?', and she waits for the answer. Its second shape is the status pair: a thing, its status, a full stop, then the next pair ('Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.'; in Hindi mode with no comma, 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।'). The item is named, never numbered: no ordinals, no counts, no prices, no clock times. THE HOME VOICE takes over the moment a family feeling arrives (a goodbye, a cousin's news, her husband worried, a report): the statuses stop, and she speaks short whole sentences of plain, warm Hindi with their hai or hoon ('Fikr mat karo. Mummy ji ka BP normal hai.', 'Mujhe yakeen hai.', 'Ab kya karna hai?'). A city manager talks in statuses at the desk and stops at home, and so does she, which is why the desk voice is funny when she turns it on her husband and used in no tender moment. A bubble runs 4 to 10 words, most often 6 to 9; usually one bubble, at most two. Crisp, unhurried and never raised: no exclamation mark in any bubble, 'Congratulations.' and 'Ish.' included, and never the shout (the chapter's shout is Mama ji's). The same pace in a crisis as at tea, which is why people calm down near her. Firm with vendors, polite with elders, sly with her husband. Talked over, she raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes when the room is quiet. When cross she goes slower, turns the clipboard round to face the person, reads the line aloud from it ('Yahan likha hai.') and closes with an icy 'Thank you' to a vendor, or a flat 'Correct?' to family. Apart from the cast: not Mummy's comma lists of jobs and people with no status ('Aur kuch?') or her home things in counter English; not Mausa ji's subjectless verdicts on things; not Captain sahab's call then reason; not Papa's whole sentences with a time in them; not Nani's jobs handed to 'koi'; not Mama ji's run-ons and 'Oho!'. A script can count it: about half her lines carry a status word or end on 'Correct?', and every one of those is about a job, a list or a vendor; her family feeling lines carry none, and most of them have hai or hoon; no line carries an ordinal, a figure or '!'.
voice.mix: City whole-clause switching, the younger urban pattern in the realism notes (the Dehradun code-switching study): she switches at the full stop, a whole Hindi clause and then a whole English one, or the other way round ('Meri shaadi ki bhi list thi. Still on file.'). Inside a Hindi clause the desk crosses over in two ways: its nouns (list, item, form, file, claim, receipt, balance, payment) and, as with most city people under fifty, an office English verb with kar or ho ('List ab tum handle karo.', 'Claim main file karti hoon.', 'Receipt pe sign kar dijiye.', 'Bahut help ho gayi.'). Her English verbs come from the office (file, sign, check, handle, note), never from the home: Mummy turns home things into counter English ('MCB check karo', 'mains off karo'), and Mama ji talks logistics. Her English statuses in Hinglish: done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, still on file, all clear, correct. In Hindi mode a status becomes the everyday Hindi a city office speaks (हो गया, लग गया, बाक़ी, पता नहीं, मंज़ूर, चालू, बंद, ठीक, फ़ाइल में), with पेंडिंग and स्टेटस kept only for her two dry jokes, and with no comma between a Hindi subject and its verb, because spoken Hindi does not pause there; a colon comes only before a label with no verb ('स्टेटस: मेहमान।', 'तुम्हारे मामा जी: अब भी पेंडिंग।'). The commas stay in Hinglish and English pairs. Her Hindi carries people, food, rooms and elders, and the town's everyday Urdu-rooted words sit in it as they do in anyone's (fikr, zaroor, yakeen). 'Thank you' and 'Sorry' are the counter's words, English in every mode (थैंक यू, सॉरी), for vendors and strangers only; with family her sorry is Hindi ('मुझसे छूट गया') and her thanks is plain ('बहुत मदद हो गई'). Polite Hindi to every elder and every vendor (आप, -इए). One Bengali word, her mother's: the exclamation 'Ish.' Nothing else from Bengali, and never a spelled accent. Apart from Mama ji, who leads with fast English and runs his clauses together on 'aur haan', she is clause by clause, each one closed, and her English is the desk's, never logistics talk, slang or 'Don't worry'.
tics: THE READBACK, her lead tic, for jobs and plans: 'So.', your plan in one whole sentence, 'Correct?', and she waits: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ आज रात से तुम्हारे पास। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?'. From Friday she stops reading your plan back to you, and that is her deepest thank-you, the one she never says.

THE STATUS PAIR, for the list and for vendors: thing, comma, status, full stop: 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Keys, not known.' In Hindi mode the comma goes and the status is everyday Hindi: 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी।' She names the item, never its place on the list.

THE SWITCH HOME: when a family feeling arrives, the desk finishes its line and plain Hindi, most often with hai or hoon, says the thing that matters: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?'; 'Congratulations. Joining kab se? Somvaar? Bahut achha.' No status, file, tick or 'Correct?' in a goodbye, a congratulation, comfort or a report.
She files herself as a joke, never as a feeling. Asked how she is: 'Main? Sab clear hai.' | 'मैं? सब ठीक है।' | 'Me? All clear.' Hurt, said once and dry: 'Status: mehmaan.'

Asks every vendor and helper about their children, the counter's habit and her one interest on the page that is not a list: 'Bhaiya ji, beti ka paper kaisa gaya?'. It is also, quietly, about her own daughter.

'Thank you' and 'Sorry' out loud, in English, to every vendor and stranger, even when cross: the counter's words. Never to family (Mausi teases her for saying it 'like a bill'); thanked at home, she says 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.'
Thanks family in plain words, 'Bahut help ho gayi.', and her husband the everyday way, 'Maan gayi.'; at most once a chapter the pen comes down on a spoken 'Tick.'.

Sly about her husband, said as a status and to the young ones, as if he were not standing there: 'Your Mama ji: still pending.' Once a chapter at most, so it stays a joke and is not her only one: his count, his dinner and the rest get the plain line.

The house's common fillers, like anyone in it: achha, suno, arre, theek hai, chalo, chaliye, to open a line or in the middle of one ('Achha, suno. List ab tum handle karo.'). She owns none of them; her shape is what marks her.
Talked over: raises the pen, point up, says nothing, and finishes when the room is quiet. ('Ek minute' is yours, so she never says it.)
Never a rhetorical or a stacked question (those are Mausi's); every question she asks has one answer, and she waits for it.
Days of the week, never a clock time and never 'soon' as a promise: 'by Saturday', 'Thursday evening'. (At a parting she asks 'Agli baar kab?' and waits for a day.)
No exclamation mark anywhere, spoken or typed, not even for 'Ish.' or 'Congratulations.'
catchphrases: THE READBACK: 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | 'तो। चाबियाँ आज रात से तुम्हारे पास। सही?' | 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?' (the line people quote back)

THE STATUS PAIR: 'Keys, pending. Envelopes, done.' | 'चाबियाँ अभी बाक़ी। लिफ़ाफ़े हो गए।' | 'Chaabiyan, pending. Lifafe, done.' (writers keep it away from any decision whose cards use keys or envelopes, rule 36)

HER NO: 'Not on the list.' | 'लिस्ट में नहीं है।' | 'List mein nahin hai.' Turned round once, at the first slice, laughing and with no exclamation: 'That wasn't on my list.' | 'ये मेरी लिस्ट में नहीं था।' | 'Ye meri list mein nahin tha.' (None of the three carries a number.)
HER HOUSE RULE: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'
voice.exclamation: 'Ish.' | 'इश्श।' | 'Ish.' (kept as 'Ish.' in English mode too, as her own sound). Her mother's Bengali word, for dismay and sympathy only ('oh no', 'oh dear'): the power cut, a child's fever, a spilt glass, a dropped tray. Never for good news, a laugh or a happy surprise: Hindi-mode players know the coy 'इश्श' of old Hindi films, and on a laugh it would read as that, so at the first slice she just laughs and says the line, and good news gets her home voice. Said flat and low, closed with a full stop, never with '!', never with a giggle or a hand to the mouth. No religious meaning. At most once a scene. Nobody else in the cast uses it, and it leans to one region on purpose, her mother's. Two reader checks: a Bengali reader confirms the sense; a Hindi-first reader confirms it is not heard as ईश ('lord', a word rule 3 bans; ईश has a long ई and one श, इश्श a short इ and a doubled श) and that, kept to dismay, it does not read as the filmi coy sound. Many Hindi-first players may hear the coy 'इश्श' whatever the context, so the fallback for Hindi mode is written and ready, and Hindi mode keeps 'इश्श' only if the Hindi-first reader clears it. 'Ish' stays in Hinglish and English, where the Bengali sense survives. In Hindi mode 'अजीब।' takes its place where the dismay is at a thing ('अजीब। बत्ती चली गई।'); where it is sympathy for a person, Hindi mode drops the sound and opens on the care ('बच्चे का बुख़ार उतरा, भैया जी?', 'आस्तीन गीली हुई? कागज़ मैं उठा लेती हूँ।'), since 'अजीब' said to a sick or upset child sounds like a judgement. If the Bengali reader fails it too, 'Ajeeb.' | 'Odd.' goes into the other two modes the same way. Nobody else in the cast uses 'Ajeeb'.
voice.sorry_thanks_love: SORRY, TO FAMILY: plain everyday Hindi, then the right entry at once, aloud: 'Mujhse chhoot gaya, Didi. Shanivaar likhiye.' | 'मुझसे छूट गया, दीदी। शनिवार लिखिए।' | 'I missed that, Didi. Please write Saturday.' SORRY, TO VENDORS AND STRANGERS: the counter's English word, then the fact put right: 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji, mujhse galat likh gaya. Payment Shanivaar ko.' | 'सॉरी, भैया जी, मुझसे ग़लत लिख गया। पेमेंट शनिवार को।' | 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji, I wrote it down wrong. Payment's on Saturday.' Hers is told apart from Mausi's doubled 'Sorry, sorry!' with food and Mama ji's 'Sorry, Didi, poora kasoor mera!' by its size: one plain sentence and the correction, the blame never made bigger. THANKS, GIVEN: to family, plain words, 'Bahut help ho gayi.' | 'बहुत मदद हो गई।' | 'That was a big help.' ('Badi Didi, aapke aane se bahut help ho gayi.'); to her husband, when he turns out right, the everyday 'Maan gayi.' | 'मान गई।' | 'I'll give you that.'; at most once a chapter, the pen comes down on a spoken 'Tick.'; to vendors and strangers, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.', English in every mode; to you, besides the words, from Friday she stops reading your plan back, and her typed lists to you lose their 'Correct?' line. THANKS, RECEIVED: from family, the real brush-off of an Indian house, where a thank-you between relatives sounds too formal: 'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.'; from a vendor, 'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' back. CONGRATULATIONS: 'Congratulations.' in Hinglish and English, 'बधाई हो।' in Hindi mode, with a full stop, then the one practical question she cannot help ('Joining kab se?'). LOVE: plain and short at a parting, once the desk has finished its line: 'Ticket, tiffin, done. Agli baar kab?' | 'टिकट, टिफ़िन, सब रख दिया। अगली बार कब?' | 'Ticket, tiffin, done. When will you come next?', the one question she cannot help, and she waits for a day. Otherwise never in feeling words, and left open: the one line she never ticks, 'Beti ka bag', at the top of every wedding list, and the pen held over it on the wedding evening; Mama ji's item, which she always ticks first, and his hand, the only one allowed to write on her list.
uses: status words, for jobs, lists and vendors: done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, still on file, all clear | हो गया, लग गया, बाक़ी, पता नहीं, मंज़ूर, चालू, बंद, ठीक, फ़ाइल में (no comma before them in Hindi) | done, pending, not known, safe, approved, in progress, closed, still on file, all clear (English in Hinglish)

the desk's nouns: item, list, form, file, claim, receipt, balance, payment, advance | आइटम, लिस्ट, फ़ॉर्म, फ़ाइल, क्लेम, रसीद, बाक़ी, पेमेंट, एडवांस | item, list, form, file, claim, receipt, balance, payment, advance
office English verbs with kar or ho: handle karo, file karti hoon, sign kar dijiye, check kar lijiye, note kar lo, help ho gayi | सँभालो, भरती हूँ, साइन कर दीजिए, चेक कर लीजिए, लिख लो, मदद हो गई

'Not on the list.' | 'लिस्ट में नहीं है।' | 'List mein nahin hai.' (her no)
'It's written here.' | 'यहाँ लिखा है।' | 'Yahan likha hai.' (her anger, the clipboard turned round)

'Status: not known.' | 'अभी पता नहीं।' | 'Status not known.', then a check at the source the way the desk does it (a notice on the shop, the receipt), for rumours about things only, never about a person
'Main? Sab clear hai.' | 'मैं? सब ठीक है।' | 'Me? All clear.' (herself, filed as a joke)
'Bahut help ho gayi.' | 'बहुत मदद हो गई।' | 'That was a big help.' (thanks to family); 'Tick.' at most once a chapter
'Ghar mein thank you nahin chalta.' | 'घर में थैंक यू नहीं चलता।' | 'No thank-yous at home.' (thanked by family)
'Thank you, Bhaiya ji.' and 'Sorry, Bhaiya ji.' (the counter's words, English in every mode, to vendors and strangers)
'Mujhse chhoot gaya.' | 'मुझसे छूट गया।' | 'I missed that.' (sorry to family)
'Congratulations.' | 'बधाई हो।' | 'Congratulations.'
'Agli baar kab?' | 'अगली बार कब?' | 'When will you come next?' (at a parting, and she waits for a day)
'Maan gayi.' | 'मान गई।' | 'I'll give you that.' (to her husband, when he is right)
the house's common fillers: achha, suno, arre, theek hai, chalo, chaliye | अच्छा, सुनो, अरे, ठीक है, चलो, चलिए
the town's everyday Urdu-rooted words: fikr, zaroor, yakeen | फ़िक्र, ज़रूर, यक़ीन
'Ish.' | 'इश्श।' (her exclamation, dismay and sympathy only)
'your Mama ji' | 'तुम्हारे मामा जी' and 'your Nani' | 'तुम्हारी नानी' (to the young ones)
questions about other people's children: exams, results, fevers | पेपर, रिज़ल्ट, बुख़ार | paper, result, bukhaar
days of the week: by Saturday, Thursday evening | शनिवार तक, गुरुवार शाम | Shanivaar tak, Guruvaar shaam
never: Ordinals or counts in speech: pehla, doosra, teesra, chautha; first, second, third; 'Item four'; 'One, keys' (ordinals belong to nobody, matrix 2.15)
A figure of her own in any bubble: no count, price or clock time (the number leaners are Papa and Tinku); she does not even repeat Mama ji's figure back

The shrugs: maybe, perhaps, whatever, we'll see, 'chalta hai' meaning it'll do, 'adjust kar lenge' meaning we'll make do | शायद, जो भी, देखते हैं, चलता है | shayad, jo bhi, dekhte hain, chalta hai. (Her 'thank you nahin chalta' is a house rule, not a shrug, and 'adjust kijiye' as an ask to a vendor is fine.)

The desk voice in a family feeling moment: no status, file, tick or 'Correct?' in a goodbye, a congratulation, comfort or a report ('Your file: open. Always.' and 'Naukri, done. Tick.' are struck for this)

Other people's owned phrases, and their exclamations as her habitual cry, never their fillers (a cry said now and then is free): Mausa ji's one-word 'Lo.' and 'Theek.' (and the Bengali 'Thik ache', the same word) and 'Mazboot'; Nani's closer 'Bas.', her 'Aur tum.' and 'Khush raho'; Captain sahab's 'Arre waah.'; Mausi's 'Suno, suno, suno!', 'Haay', 'hai na?', a tripled word and 'Bahut yaad'; Mama ji's 'Oho', 'Don't worry', 'aur haan' run-ons, 'full' and 'No problem'; Mummy's 'Had hai!', 'Aur kuch?' and 'mere khaate mein'; Papa's 'Kamaal', 'Noted', 'Confirmed', 'Reached?' and 'sharp'; Tinku's 'Gazab', scores and, at a parting, her 'Jaldi aana'; Masterji's 'Uff'; yours 'Badhiya', 'sorted', 'Ek minute' and 'Pehle ___'
'Mubarak ho' (unused for now: it and 'Badhai ho' are both everyday congratulations and take one ruling, and an Urdu-speaking reader checks that both sides are treated alike, India verdict 3)
'Ish' on good news, a laugh or a happy surprise
'What will people say?' | 'लोग क्या कहेंगे?': it is her fear, so she never says it
an exclamation mark, a rhetorical or stacked question, a shout bubble
'Thank you' or the English 'sorry' to family; 'How are you?' to you

Proof words in any chapter that holds a report twin: 'Is it in writing?', likhit, saboot, proof, notice (build flag for proof words near a report beat), and never a doubt about a person (rule 22, anti-persona A2); after a report no pen is raised and no word of writing it down ('kya likhoon', 'note karo'), which the player's and Tinku's files fence the same way
'Mummy ji' for Nani in a line to you, which reads as your own Mummy; to the young ones it is 'tumhari Nani'

any religious word or exclamation (rule 3 and matrix 2.13: no Hai Ram, Bhagwan, Allah, Rab, Wahe Guru, Jesus, Ishwar, Mata ji as a goddess; in English mode no Gosh, Goodness, Heavens, Lord, Thank God), any caste word (रसोइया, never हलवाई), any brand

beta, bhaiya, didi or any word for you that fixes gender (rule 8); any Hindi form with you as the doer that marks gender (rule 66: no -ोगे/-ोगी, no -ेगा/-ेगी, no आ गए/आ गईं, no कर रहे/रही हो, no -ते/-ती रहो); her asks to you are commands and subjunctives ('बोलो', 'चाबियाँ कौन रखे?')
'phone' | 'फ़ोन' or 'call' | 'कॉल' in any chapter 5 bubble, a card person's name or a card note's words in any bubble (rule 36)

anything that doubts a report of harassment or a dowry demand, or calls one a misunderstanding (rule 22): she believes it at once and asks what to do now; a gift demand as a list item, anything for the groom's side, anything listed as going in her daughter's bag
a word about a woman's clothes, looks or conduct, the bride's looks, or anyone's caste, community or region
slang (chill, bro, scene), 'aunty' about anyone, Bengali beyond 'Ish', any Bengali stock joke (fish, sweets, 'babu', bossy mothers)
address: YOU: तुम, only in commands ('लिस्ट तुम सँभालो', 'बोलो'), 'who should' asks in the subjunctive ('चाबियाँ कौन रखे?'), possessives that agree with the thing owned ('चाबियाँ तुम्हारे पास', 'तुम्हारी नानी') and verbless status lines ('Keys, yours.'). Never a past or a future with you as the doer. No name, no beta, no family word; she often starts with the item, not with 'you'. You say 'Mami' and आप: 'Mami, dikhaiye.' | 'मामी, दिखाइए।' | 'Let's see, Mami.' (your file).

NANI: 'Mummy ji' | 'मम्मी जी', आप and -इए ('Mummy ji, aap baithiye.'), to her face and to Mama ji; to the young ones she says 'tumhari Nani' | 'तुम्हारी नानी', as she says 'tumhare Mama ji', so the line never reads as their own Mummy. Nani says आप back to her ('Do sit.') until December's first तुम. She greets Nani by bending from the hips and taking her hand in both of hers.
MUMMY: 'Didi' | 'दीदी', आप. Mummy calls her 'Bhabhi' and says तुम.
MAUSI: 'Badi Didi' | 'बड़ी दीदी', आप. Mausi calls her 'Bhabhi' and says तुम.
PAPA: 'Jija ji' | 'जीजा जी', आप; he says आप to her and no name.
MAUSA JI: 'Bade Jija ji' | 'बड़े जीजा जी', आप, her husband's word for him, as the cast map's address table settles it.
MAMA JI: no name; तुम both ways; to the young ones, drily, 'your Mama ji' | 'तुम्हारे मामा जी'. He calls her 'Boss' (his file, an owner question).
TINKU: 'Tinku', तुम. Tinku says 'Mami' and आप.
MASTERJI and CAPTAIN SAHAB: by their titles, आप.

VENDORS AND HELPERS: men 'Bhaiya ji' | 'भैया जी' (Mummy says plain 'ji', Mama ji '[Name] bhai'), women by their name and 'ji' once she has asked it, which she always does, and आप to both, always, even when angry, with 'Thank you' at the end.
STRANGERS AT ANY COUNTER: आप, 'Thank you' and, when she is at fault, 'Sorry'.
HER DAUGHTER: 'my daughter' | 'मेरी बेटी' and nothing more in any bubble; 'Beti ka bag' only on her typed list.
samples: GIVING AN ORDER, 5.03 (revised, to you at the blue gate, Mama ji beside her; one bubble: the status joke about his count is cut, since her one joke about him is the gate greeting; his count has just been said aloud, so she needs no figure of her own): EN 'Right, listen. You run the list now.' | Hinglish 'Achha, suno. List ab tum handle karo.' | Hindi 'अच्छा, सुनो। लिस्ट अब तुम सँभालो।'

THE READBACK, 5.04 (to you, the day's job list card held out in both hands; her lead habit): EN 'So. Keys with you, from tonight. Correct?' | Hinglish 'Toh. Chaabiyan tumhare paas, aaj raat se. Sahi?' | Hindi 'तो। चाबियाँ आज रात से तुम्हारे पास। सही?'

THE DAY'S STATUS (to you, Thursday morning; the status pair, with no comma in Hindi): EN 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Keys, not known.' | Hinglish 'Tent, done. Cook, pending. Chaabiyan, not known.' | Hindi 'टेंट लग गया। रसोइया अभी बाक़ी। चाबियों का पता नहीं।'

WORRYING (to you, Thursday night; the switch falls at the full stop): EN 'Envelopes, still pending. And it's Thursday.' | Hinglish 'Lifafe, still pending. Aur aaj Guruvaar hai.' | Hindi 'लिफ़ाफ़े अब भी बाक़ी। और आज गुरुवार है।'

SAYING NO (the tent man, polite to the end): EN 'More tents, Bhaiya ji? Not on the list. Thank you.' | Hinglish 'Aur tent, Bhaiya ji? List mein nahin hai. Thank you.' | Hindi 'और टेंट, भैया जी? लिस्ट में नहीं है। थैंक यू।'

LOSING HER TEMPER (the tent man; slower, the clipboard turned round to face him, the line read from it, and her icy counter thanks to close; two bubbles): EN 'It's written here, Bhaiya ji. habits: DEVICE: a large-screen smartphone in a plain navy-blue case, text at the normal size, kept in her bag and out only for a call (at her right ear, the pen slid into the clipboard's clip) or for the night's list. Two quick thumbs. A plain power bank for everyone else's phones. In chapter 5 her phone stays off screen, like Mama ji's.

SCRIPT: Roman letters only, in the city's Hinglish: English items and statuses, Hindi people and verbs, and the office verbs with kar ('Rooms done. Chaabiyan kiske paas?', 'Envelopes Tinku ko handover karo'). Never Devanagari, which is too slow for her. Devanagari versions are given in case the owner applies rule 65 to typed messages; they drop the comma between a thing and its status, as her spoken Hindi does. Her lines to you mark no gender ('You take over Thu evening').

FORMAT: one item per line, a capitalised noun and its status symbol, with a comma before any detail ('Keys, yours ✅'). No line numbers and no digits in any message on screen: that is the typing half of the number cap. No full stops at line ends, no whole words in capitals (capitals read as shouting, realism), no exclamation mark. The first line names the list and the day ('Wedding list, Thu'). On every wedding list the second line is 'Beti ka bag', with no symbol, the only line she never gives a status; then 'Papa, trains ✅', the one item she never has to chase. Family lists end on 'Correct?'; vendor lists end on 'Thank you'.

APART FROM THE OTHERS: Papa types single facts with full stops and times, Mummy lowercase one-liners that end on a figure, Tinku lowercase stretched letters and scores, and you the lowercase colon form ('keys: sorted'), which is why her detail takes a comma, not a colon.
STATUS SYMBOLS, her only emoji: ✅ done, ⏳ pending, ❓ not known. No faces and no hands (👍 is Mummy's; the folded hands wait on the owner), no stickers.
VERSIONS: she never sends a correction; she resends the whole list with 'revised' after the day ('Wedding list, Thu, revised'), so the header carries no figure. On screen, one message card at a time.

THE THANK-YOU IN TYPE: from Friday her lists to you drop the closing 'Correct?' line. Nobody else's list ever does. To family she types no thank-you, as she says none; every vendor list ends on 'Thank you'.
TIMING: lists go out at eleven at night, after her shift and dinner; in the day she replies within the minute; if 'Correct?' has no answer, she rings.
VOICE NOTES: never sends one ('you cannot tick a voice note'); when one comes, such as Mausi's long ones, she replies with a summary list of it ending on 'Correct?'.
FORWARDS: none, ever. Her one reply to a forward: a single ✅ under Papa's good-morning flower, every morning, the only reply he gets.
CALLS: Nani is rung, never texted, every evening since May for the BP; vendors are rung first and then sent a list of what was agreed, ending 'Thank you'.
FIGURES: the monthly BP log she sends Nani's doctor is the one thing she types with figures in it, and it stays off screen.
TYPOS: none; she rereads every list before sending; autocorrect on.

ON SCREEN: single messages only, as live text on a painted blank phone or a message card (rules 30 and 40); no app look, no 'forwarded' or 'edited' label, no group chat on screen (owner, 23 Oct). The Sunday list to you is the one worth showing, early in chapter 5 if the writers have room, because it is where the player first sees the line with no status.
